title: Number System
summary: Divisibility, remainders, unit digits, factors and recurring decimals — the base layer every other Quant topic uses. CGL asks 1–3 direct questions per Tier 1 shift (missing-digit divisibility, remainders and unit digit are near-certain) and a few more in Tier 2.

subtopics.title: Number types, place value & counting
subtopics.concept: Numbers come in families: natural, whole, integers, rational and irrational. A prime has exactly two factors, and co-prime numbers share only the factor 1. This subtopic also covers place value, counting multiples in a range, sums of standard series, and reversed two-digit numbers.

tricks.body: Count multiples of k up to the end of the range, then subtract the multiples before the start. No listing needed.

tricks.title: Place value in one product
tricks.body: Place value minus face value equals digit times (position value minus 1). The 9999 pattern does it in one line.

steps: Digit $8$ sits in the ten-thousands place: place value $= 8 \times 10000 = 80000$.

tricks.body: For any evenly spaced list, the sum equals the number of terms times the middle term. The middle term is the average of first and last.

mistakes.wrong: Counting the end points when the question says between.
mistakes.right: Between 1 and 100 means 2 to 99. From 1 to 100 includes both ends.

mistakes.wrong: Treating 1 as a prime number.
mistakes.right: 1 is neither prime nor composite, and 2 is the only even prime.

mistakes.wrong: In 'divisible by 3 or 5' questions, adding both counts and stopping.
mistakes.right: Add both counts, then subtract the multiples of 15 once.

mistakes.wrong: Using the sum formula for a series that starts away from 1.
mistakes.right: Find the full sum up to the end, then subtract the sum before the start.

mistakes.wrong: Reading 'divisible by 4 and 6' as divisible by 24.
mistakes.right: It means divisible by LCM(4, 6) = 12. Join 'and' divisors through their LCM.

subtopics.notes:
Every number in the exam belongs to one or more families. This lesson covers the families, prime and co-prime numbers, place value, counting multiples in a range, sums of standard series, page numbering, and reversed two-digit numbers. These are quick one-mark questions, so speed matters most.

### The number families

| Family | Members | Watch point |
|---|---|---|
| Natural | $1, 2, 3, \ldots$ | $0$ is not natural |
| Whole | $0, 1, 2, \ldots$ | smallest whole number is $0$ |
| Integers | $\ldots, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, \ldots$ | $0$ is neither positive nor negative |
| Rational | $\dfrac{p}{q}$ with $q \ne 0$ | terminating and repeating decimals qualify |
| Irrational | never ends, never repeats | $\sqrt{2}$ and $\pi$; sums can still be rational |
| Real | rational and irrational together | every point on the number line |

> **Watch:** $0$ is whole but not natural, and $1$ is neither prime nor composite. Both lines appear as free marks.

### Prime, composite and co-prime
A prime has exactly two factors: $1$ and itself. A composite number has more than two factors. $2$ is the only even prime, and there are $25$ primes below $100$. Co-prime numbers share only the factor $1$: $8$ and $15$ are co-prime though neither is prime. Consecutive integers are always co-prime.

To test whether a number is prime, divide it by every prime up to its square root. For $221$ the square root is below $15$, and $221 = 13 \times 17$, so it is composite.

### Place value and face value
The face value of a digit is the digit itself. The place value is the digit times the value of its position. In $5,63,847$ the digit $6$ sits in the ten-thousands place, so its place value is $6 \times 10000 = 60000$ while its face value is $6$.

> **Rule:** Place value $-$ face value $=$ digit $\times$ (position value $- 1$). For $8$ in $9,28,475$: $8 \times 9999 = 79992$.

### Counting multiples in a range
Multiples of $k$ up to $n$ number exactly the whole-number part of $n \div k$. For a range, count up to the end and subtract the count before the start.

> **Rule:** Multiples of $k$ from $a$ to $b$ = $\left\lfloor \dfrac{b}{k} \right\rfloor - \left\lfloor \dfrac{a-1}{k} \right\rfloor$. Multiples of $7$ from $100$ to $300$: $42 - 14 = 28$.

Read the joining word with care. "Divisible by $4$ and $6$" means divisible by $\mathrm{LCM}(4, 6) = 12$, not by $24$. "Divisible by $4$ or $6$" adds the two counts and subtracts the multiples of $12$. "Neither" takes the total minus the "or" count.

### Sums of common series

| Series | Sum |
|---|---|
| $1 + 2 + \cdots + n$ | $\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$ |
| $1^2 + 2^2 + \cdots + n^2$ | $\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$ |
| $1^3 + 2^3 + \cdots + n^3$ | $\left[\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\right]^2$ |
| first $n$ odd numbers | $n^2$ |
| first $n$ even numbers | $n(n+1)$ |

For a sum that starts late, find the full sum and subtract the missing head. For $11^2$ to $20^2$: the sum up to $20$ is $2870$, the sum up to $10$ is $385$, and the answer is $2485$.

> **Tip:** Any evenly spaced list sums to: number of terms $\times$ (first $+$ last) $\div 2$. Evens from $12$ to $48$: $19$ terms, sum $19 \times 30 = 570$.

### Digits used in page numbering
Pages $1$ to $9$ use $9$ digits. Pages $10$ to $99$ use $90 \times 2 = 180$ digits. Each later page uses as many digits as it has. For $350$ pages: $9 + 180 + 251 \times 3 = 942$ digits. The reverse question subtracts $189$, divides by $3$, and adds $99$ to the quotient.

### Two-digit numbers and their reverse
Write the number as $10a + b$; its reverse is $10b + a$. Their difference is $9(a - b)$ and their sum is $11(a + b)$. A number that exceeds its reverse by $27$ has digits differing by $27 \div 9 = 3$. For example $74$ and $47$ differ by $27$.

patterns.name: Counting numbers divisible by k in a range
patterns.howToSpot: A range is given and the question asks how many numbers in it are divisible by one or two given numbers. Words like and, or, neither or but not decide the method.
steps: For one divisor $k$: count multiples up to the end, then subtract the multiples before the start.
For 'by $x$ and $y$': count with $k = \mathrm{LCM}(x, y)$ instead of $x \times y$.
For 'by $x$ or $y$': add both counts, then subtract the count of the LCM once.
For 'neither': subtract the 'or' count from the size of the range.
patterns.why: Every k-th number is a multiple of k, so floor division counts them without any listing.

example.q: How many numbers from 1 to 300 are divisible by 4 or 6?

patterns.name: Sum of a series or of multiples in a range
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks for a sum: all two-digit multiples of a number, squares from one point to another, or the first n odd numbers.
steps: Count the terms: for multiples of $d$ from $a$ to $l$, the count is $\dfrac{l - a}{d} + 1$.
Add the first and last terms and halve the total to get the average.
For squares or cubes, take the full sum formula and subtract the head you do not need.
patterns.why: Pairing first with last, second with second-last, and so on gives equal totals, so the sum is the count times the average.

example.q: Find the sum of all two-digit multiples of 7.

patterns.name: Place value and face value
patterns.howToSpot: A number is written with Indian commas and the question asks for the place value, the face value, or a combination of both for one digit.
steps: Mark positions from the right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, lakhs.
Place value $=$ digit $\times$ that position's value. Face value $=$ the digit itself.
Do the asked operation: sum, difference or product.
patterns.why: Our system is positional, so the same digit is worth ten times more in each step to the left.

example.q: Find the difference between the place value and the face value of 5 in 8,45,327.
steps: Digit $5$ is in the thousands place: place value $= 5 \times 1000 = 5000$.

patterns.name: Classifying numbers: prime, rational, co-prime
patterns.howToSpot: Options list numbers and the question asks which one is prime, rational, irrational, or co-prime with another.
steps: Test primes by dividing by every prime up to the square root of the number.
Simplify before classifying: a product of surds can collapse to a rational number.
Co-prime just needs HCF 1; neither number has to be prime.
patterns.why: A number is irrational only if its simplified value still has a decimal that never ends and never repeats.

example.q: Is 407 a prime number?
steps: $\sqrt{407}$ is just above $20$, so test primes up to $20$.
Two factors besides 1, so it is composite.

patterns.name: Digits used in page numbering
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks how many digits a book of N pages needs, or gives the digit count and asks for the pages.
steps: Pages 1 to 9 use 9 digits at one digit each.
Pages beyond 99 use one digit per digit of the page number; multiply and add.
For the reverse question, strip 9 and 180 first, then divide what remains.
patterns.why: Each block of page numbers has a fixed digit length, so the count splits into three clean parts.

example.q: How many digits are used to number the pages of a 200-page book?

patterns.name: Two-digit numbers and digit reversal
patterns.howToSpot: The digits of a two-digit number are reversed and the number changes by a known amount, or consecutive numbers are summed.
steps: Write the number as $10a + b$ with $a$ the tens digit and $b$ the units digit.
A reversal difference divided by 9 gives the digit difference $a - b$.
A reversal sum divided by 11 gives the digit sum $a + b$.
For consecutive numbers, divide the sum by the count to get the middle number.
patterns.why: The tens digit is worth ten times the units digit, so a swap moves 9 per unit of digit difference.

example.q: A two-digit number exceeds the number formed by reversing its digits by 27. What is the difference between its digits?

revision: Multiples of $k$ from $a$ to $b$: $\left\lfloor \dfrac{b}{k} \right\rfloor - \left\lfloor \dfrac{a-1}{k} \right\rfloor$.
'And' means the LCM; 'or' means add counts and subtract the LCM count.
Sum formulas: $\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}$, $\dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$, $\left[\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}\right]^2$, $n^2$ for odd numbers.
Place value $-$ face value $=$ digit $\times$ (position value $- 1$).
Reversal: difference $= 9(a-b)$, sum $= 11(a+b)$.
$0$ is whole but not natural; $1$ is neither prime nor composite.

subtopics.title: Divisibility rules
subtopics.concept: A number is divisible by d when d divides it with remainder 0. Quick tests exist for 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10 and 11, and composite divisors split into co-prime parts. Powers follow their own rules: a to the n minus b to the n is always divisible by a minus b.

formulas.name: Composite divisor
formulas.tex: pq \mid N \iff p \mid N \text{ and } q \mid N, \quad \gcd(p, q) = 1

formulas.name: Difference of even powers
formulas.tex: (a + b) \mid (a^n - b^n) \text{ when } n \text{ is even}

formulas.name: Sum of odd powers
formulas.tex: (a + b) \mid (a^n + b^n) \text{ when } n \text{ is odd}

tricks.title: Split into co-prime factors
tricks.body: Break the divisor into parts with no common factor and test each part separately. Order the tests from the most restrictive first.

example.q: If the five-digit number 37x84 is divisible by 12, find the smallest value of x.
steps: $12 = 3 \times 4$. By $4$: last two digits $84$ already pass, for any $x$.
By $3$: digit sum $3 + 7 + x + 8 + 4 = 22 + x$ must be a multiple of $3$.

tricks.title: The repeated-block family
tricks.body: Any six-digit number abcabc equals abc times 1001, so it is always divisible by 7, 11 and 13.

example.q: Which of 7, 11 and 13 divide 484484?

tricks.title: Sum of odd powers
tricks.body: For a to the n plus b to the n with odd n, check the options against a plus b first. No expansion is ever needed.

example.q: Is 17 to the power 25 plus 23 to the power 25 divisible by 40?
steps: The exponent $25$ is odd, so $a^n + b^n$ is divisible by $a + b$.

mistakes.wrong: Splitting a composite divisor into parts that share a factor, like 12 = 2 x 6.
mistakes.right: Use co-prime parts only: 12 = 3 x 4. A number can pass 2 and 6 yet fail 12.

mistakes.wrong: Checking only the last two digits for divisibility by 8.
mistakes.right: The rule of 8 needs the last three digits.

mistakes.wrong: For 11, forgetting that the difference of the two sums can be 0 or negative.
mistakes.right: Accept 0, 11, 22 and also -11 as valid differences.

mistakes.wrong: Using the (a + b) rule for a to the n plus b to the n when n is even.
mistakes.right: That rule needs odd n. For even n only a minus b divides the difference.

mistakes.wrong: Multiplying the two rules' answers instead of checking both divisibilities.
mistakes.right: For 72 = 8 x 9 the number must pass both tests; nothing is multiplied.

subtopics.notes:
A number $N$ is divisible by $d$ when $d$ divides $N$ exactly, leaving remainder $0$. Divisibility tests let you check this without long division. This lesson covers the basic tests, composite divisors, missing digits, power rules, and reaching the nearest multiple.

### The quick tests

| Divisor | Test | Example |
|---|---|---|
| $2, 5, 10$ | last digit even, $0$ or $5$, $0$ | $4,215$ by $5$ |
| $4$ | last two digits divisible by $4$ | $7,316 \to 16$ |
| $8$ | last three digits divisible by $8$ | $91,224 \to 224$ |
| $3, 9$ | digit sum divisible by $3$ or $9$ | $6,453 \to 18$ |
| $11$ | odd-place sum minus even-place sum is $0$ or a multiple of $11$ | see below |
| $7, 11, 13$ | alternating sum of three-digit blocks | $276,276 \to 276 - 276 = 0$ |

> **Rule:** For $11$, number the digits from the right. Take (odd-place sum) $-$ (even-place sum). For $948475$: odd places $5 + 4 + 4 = 13$, even places $7 + 8 + 9 = 24$, and $24 - 13 = 11$, so it is divisible by $11$.

### Composite divisors split into co-prime parts
There is no direct rule of $72$. Split the divisor into parts that share no factor, then check each part. Useful splits: $12 = 3 \times 4$, $24 = 3 \times 8$, $36 = 4 \times 9$, $72 = 8 \times 9$, $88 = 8 \times 11$, $99 = 9 \times 11$.

> **Watch:** Never split $24$ as $4 \times 6$. They share the factor $2$: the number $36$ passes both tests yet leaves remainder $12$ with $24$.

### Missing digit questions
When digits are hidden as $x$ and $y$, use the rule with the fewest choices first. The rule of $8$ pins the last three digits. The rule of $11$ gives one equation, the digit sum for $9$ gives another. Several pairs may work, but the asked quantity, usually $x + y$, stays the same in every valid pair.

### Divisibility of powers
Three rules cover almost every power question:

- $a^n - b^n$ is divisible by $a - b$ for every $n$.
- $a^n - b^n$ is divisible by $a + b$ when $n$ is even.
- $a^n + b^n$ is divisible by $a + b$ when $n$ is odd.

So $29^{18} - 15^{18}$ is divisible by both $29 - 15 = 14$ and $29 + 15 = 44$, and $17^{25} + 23^{25}$ is divisible by $40$ because $25$ is odd.

For sums of powers of one base, pull out the smallest power: $3^{25} + 3^{26} + 3^{27} = 3^{25}(1 + 3 + 9) = 3^{25} \times 13$.

### Special digit patterns
- A six-digit number written as a repeated three-digit block, like $276276$, equals $\overline{abc} \times 1001$, and $1001 = 7 \times 11 \times 13$.
- A three-digit number with equal digits, like $777 = 7 \times 111$, is divisible by $37$.
- A two-digit number plus its reverse equals $11(a + b)$; the difference is $9(a - b)$.
- The product of three consecutive integers is divisible by $6$.

### Divisibility by seven
Cut the last digit, double it, and subtract from what remains. Repeat until the number is small. If the result is divisible by $7$, so was the original: $3598 \to 359 - 16 = 343 = 7 \times 49$.

### Reaching the nearest multiple
To make $N$ divisible by $d$, divide and find the remainder $r$. Subtract $r$ to go down to the lower multiple, or add $d - r$ to go up. For $8357 \div 12$ the remainder is $5$, so adding $7$ gives $8364 = 12 \times 697$.

> **Example:** Largest four-digit multiple of a divisor: take $9999$, divide, and subtract the remainder from $9999$.

patterns.name: Missing digits for a composite divisor
patterns.howToSpot: A number with blanks x and y is said to be divisible by 72, 88, 99 or 36, and the options are values of x + y or x - y.
steps: Split the divisor into co-prime factors.
Apply the rule with fewer choices first: $8$ fixes the last three digits, $11$ gives one equation.
Feed that result into the second rule, the digit sum for $9$ or the alternating sum for $11$.
List the working pairs; the asked sum or difference is the same in all of them.
patterns.why: A number divisible by two co-prime numbers is divisible by their product, and each rule cuts the possibilities.

example.q: If the five-digit number 6x8y4 is divisible by 72, find x + y.
steps: $72 = 8 \times 9$. Rule of $8$: the last three digits $8y4$ must divide by $8$.
Rule of $9$: digit sum $6 + x + 8 + y + 4 = 18 + x + y$ must divide by $9$.

patterns.name: Divisibility by 11 with a missing digit
patterns.howToSpot: A number like 7x2859 is divisible by 11 and one digit is hidden, or the options are numbers to pick from.
steps: Number the digits from the right and add the odd places and the even places separately.
Subtract the two sums; the result must be $0$ or a multiple of $11$.
Solve for the missing digit, which must stay between $0$ and $9$.
patterns.why: Ten leaves remainder minus one with eleven, so place values flip between plus and minus.

example.q: If the number 7x2859 is divisible by 11, find x.
steps: From the right, odd places: $9 + 8 + x = 17 + x$. Even places: $5 + 2 + 7 = 14$.
Difference: $(17 + x) - 14 = 3 + x$ must be $0$ or $11$.

patterns.name: Divisibility of a power of the form a to the n minus b to the n
patterns.howToSpot: Two big powers with the same exponent, added or subtracted, and the question asks which listed number divides them.
patterns.formula: (a - b) \mid (a^n - b^n);\quad (a + b) \mid (a^n - b^n) \text{ for even } n;\quad (a + b) \mid (a^n + b^n) \text{ for odd } n
steps: Note whether the powers are added or subtracted, and whether $n$ is even or odd.
Match against the options: the difference always works; the sum needs the right parity of $n$.
patterns.why: Factoring a to the n minus b to the n exposes both a minus b and, for even n, a plus b.

example.q: 29 to the power 18 minus 15 to the power 18 is divisible by which of 14 and 44?
steps: Divisible by $a - b = 14$ always, and by $a + b = 44$ because $n$ is even.

patterns.name: Sum of powers of the same base
patterns.howToSpot: A sum like 3 to the 25 plus 3 to the 26 plus 3 to the 27 appears and the question asks what divides it.
steps: Take the smallest power common to every term outside a bracket.
Add the powers inside the bracket to get one small number.
The bracket value divides the whole sum.
patterns.why: Every term shares the smallest power, and the bracket becomes a plain number.

example.q: Find a number other than a power of 3 that divides 3 to the power 15 plus 3 to the power 16 plus 3 to the power 17.
steps: So the sum equals $3^{15} \times 13$ and is divisible by $13$.

patterns.name: Least number to add or subtract to reach a multiple
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks what least number must be added to or subtracted from N so the result is divisible by d, or for the largest n-digit multiple.
steps: Divide $N$ by $d$ and note the remainder $r$.
To go down to the lower multiple, subtract $r$.
To go up to the next multiple, add $d - r$.
For the largest n-digit multiple, divide a string of nines and subtract its remainder.
patterns.why: Multiples of d sit d apart, and the remainder measures the distance to the lower one.

example.q: What least number must be added to 3286 to make it divisible by 29?

patterns.name: Special forms: repeated blocks and equal digits
patterns.howToSpot: A six-digit number repeats a three-digit block, or a three-digit number has equal digits, and the question asks what always divides it.
steps: Write the number as its block times a fixed multiplier.
Pick the option that divides the fixed multiplier.
patterns.why: The digit pattern builds a fixed multiplier no matter which digits are used.

example.q: Which of 7, 11 and 13 divide 276276?

patterns.name: Divisibility by seven
patterns.howToSpot: The divisor 7 appears with a three- or four-digit number, often in an options question asking which numbers divide it.
steps: Cut the last digit and double it.
Subtract that from the remaining front part.
Repeat until the number has two or three digits.
If the result is divisible by $7$, the original number is too.
patterns.why: Removing the last digit maps N to a smaller number with the same remainder apart from a factor, so divisibility survives.

example.q: Is 3598 divisible by 7?

revision: Last digit tests $2, 5, 10$; last two digits for $4$; last three for $8$.
Digit sum tests $3$ and $9$; alternating sums test $11$.
Composite divisor: split into co-prime parts and test each part.
$(a-b)$ always divides $a^n - b^n$; $(a+b)$ divides it when $n$ is even; $(a+b)$ divides $a^n + b^n$ when $n$ is odd.
$\overline{abcabc} = \overline{abc} \times 7 \times 11 \times 13$.
To reach a multiple: add $d - r$ or subtract $r$.

subtopics.title: Remainders & remainder theorem
subtopics.concept: Every division obeys one formula: dividend = divisor x quotient + remainder, with the remainder smaller than the divisor. Remainders of sums and products can be found from the individual remainders, and big powers repeat in cycles.

formulas.name: Division algorithm
formulas.tex: N = d \times q + r, \quad 0 \le r < d

formulas.name: Divisor-multiple rule
formulas.tex: N \equiv r \pmod{D},\ d \mid D \ \Rightarrow\ N \equiv r \pmod{d}

formulas.name: Base one less than divisor
formulas.note: 1 if n even, d - 1 if n odd

tricks.title: Make the base plus or minus one
tricks.body: Write the base as (multiple of divisor) plus or minus 1. The whole power then collapses to plus or minus 1.

example.q: Find the remainder when 15 to the power 47 is divided by 16.

tricks.title: Negative remainders for products
tricks.body: When factors sit just below the divisor, replace each by a small negative remainder and multiply those.

example.q: Find the remainder when 98 x 97 x 96 is divided by 99.

tricks.title: Divisor is a factor, just reduce
tricks.body: If the new divisor divides the old one, reduce the old remainder by the new divisor. If it does not divide it, this shortcut is not available.

example.q: A number leaves remainder 29 when divided by 56. What is the remainder when it is divided by 8?

mistakes.wrong: Leaving a negative remainder as the final answer.
mistakes.right: Add the divisor once (or twice) until the remainder is between 0 and d - 1.

mistakes.wrong: Using the divisor-multiple rule backwards, from a small divisor to a bigger one.
mistakes.right: The rule only shrinks: from divisor D to its factor d, never the other way.

mistakes.wrong: Applying Fermat when the divisor is not prime or shares a factor with the base.
mistakes.right: Fermat needs a prime divisor that does not divide the base.

mistakes.wrong: Multiplying the full big numbers before reducing.
mistakes.right: Reduce every number to its remainder first, then multiply the small values.

mistakes.wrong: Reading successive division as two separate divisions of the same number.
mistakes.right: The second division acts on the quotient of the first, so rebuild backwards from the end.

subtopics.notes:
When 47 sweets are shared among 5 children, each gets 9 and 2 are left over. Here 47 is the dividend, 5 the divisor, 9 the quotient and 2 the remainder. The remainder is always smaller than the divisor. Every question in this lesson is built on that one idea.

### The division formula
$$\text{dividend} = \text{divisor} \times \text{quotient} + \text{remainder}$$

With divisor 24, quotient 13 and remainder 17, the dividend is $24 \times 13 + 17 = 329$. Questions that give two of the four quantities in words are asking for this formula.

> **Rule:** Write the formula first, fill in what is given, and solve for the missing piece. Check that the remainder stays below the divisor.

### Remainders add and multiply
The remainder of a sum or a product equals the remainder of the sum or product of the individual remainders. Replace each big number by its remainder first, then multiply small numbers.

For $(1021 \times 1023 \times 1025) \div 17$: the remainders are $1$, $3$ and $5$, and $1 \times 3 \times 5 = 15$, so the remainder is $15$.

### Negative remainders keep numbers small
A remainder may be written as a negative number. $98$ leaves $-1$ with $99$, and $97$ leaves $-2$. So $98 \times 97 \times 96$ leaves $(-1)(-2)(-3) = -6$, and adding the divisor gives $93$.

> **Tip:** If your final remainder is negative, add the divisor once. If it is still negative, add again.

### Big powers cycle
Powers repeat their remainders. Find a small power that leaves $1$ or $-1$, then split the exponent.

- $2^3 = 8$ leaves $1$ with $7$, so $2^{100} = (2^3)^{33} \times 2$ leaves $2$.
- A base one more than the divisor always leaves $1$.
- A base one less than the divisor leaves $1$ for even powers and $d - 1$ for odd powers.
- Fermat: for a prime $p$ that does not divide the base, $a^{p-1}$ leaves $1$ with $p$.

### When the new divisor divides the old
If $N$ leaves $r$ with divisor $D$, and the new divisor $d$ is a factor of $D$, then $N$ leaves $r \bmod d$ with $d$. Since $342 = 18 \times 19$, a remainder of $47$ with $342$ means remainders $11$ with $18$ and $9$ with $19$.

> **Watch:** This works one way only. Knowing the remainder with $d$ tells you nothing about the remainder with $D$.

### Dividing successively
'Divided successively by 4 and 5 leaving remainders 1 and 2' means: divide $N$ by $4$, then divide that quotient by $5$. Rebuild from the last step: the smallest final quotient is $0$, so the middle value is $0 \times 5 + 2 = 2$ and $N = 4 \times 2 + 1 = 9$.

### Factorial sums collapse early
From $5! = 120$ onwards every factorial is a multiple of $15$. So for $1! + 2! + \cdots + 50!$ divided by $15$, only $1 + 2 + 6 + 24 = 33$ matters, and the remainder is $3$.

> **Example:** A number leaves remainder 5 with 9. Then $4N$ leaves $4 \times 5 = 20$, and $20 \bmod 9 = 2$.

patterns.name: Remainder with a factor of the old divisor
patterns.howToSpot: A number leaves a remainder with a big divisor, and the question asks for the remainder with a smaller number that divides that divisor.
patterns.formula: N = Dq + r,\ d \mid D \ \Rightarrow\ N \bmod d = r \bmod d
steps: Check that the new divisor $d$ truly divides the old divisor $D$.

subtopics.title: Unit digit & cyclicity
subtopics.concept: The unit digit of a power depends only on the unit digit of the base and on the exponent's remainder when divided by four. Unit digits of powers repeat in short cycles, so huge expressions collapse to one digit in seconds.

tricks.body: From 5! on, every factorial ends in 0, so a factorial sum's unit digit comes from the first four terms alone.

subtopics.notes:
The unit digit is the last digit of a number, the ones place. Exams ask for the unit digit of monsters like $7^{105} \times 3^{58}$, numbers far too big to compute. The rescue: the unit digit of a product depends only on the unit digits of the factors. $1237 \times 48$ ends the same way as $7 \times 8 = 56$, that is, in $6$.

### Power cycles
Write out powers of $7$: the unit digits run $7, 9, 3, 1$, then repeat. This repeat length is the cyclicity.

| Base digit | Cycle | Length |
|---|---|---|
| $0, 1, 5, 6$ | never changes | $1$ |
| $4$ | $4, 6$ | $2$ |
| $9$ | $9, 1$ | $2$ |
| $2$ | $2, 4, 8, 6$ | $4$ |
| $3$ | $3, 9, 7, 1$ | $4$ |
| $7$ | $7, 9, 3, 1$ | $4$ |
| $8$ | $8, 4, 2, 6$ | $4$ |

> **Rule:** Divide the exponent by $4$. A remainder of $1$, $2$ or $3$ means use that power; a remainder of $0$ means use the fourth power. For $4$ and $9$, only odd or even matters.

### The method step by step
Take $8^{67}$. Keep the base digit $8$. Divide $67$ by $4$: remainder $3$. The third member of the cycle of $8$ is $2$, so the unit digit is $2$. Only the last two digits of a big exponent matter, because $100$ divides by $4$.

### Products, sums and differences
Find each unit digit first, then combine. For sums, add the digits and keep the last one. For differences, subtract; if the result is negative, add $10$. For $7^{105} - 3^{58}$: the digits are $7$ and $9$, and $7 - 9 = -2$, so the answer is $10 - 2 = 8$.

> **Watch:** The digit-borrow trick for a difference assumes the first number really is the larger one. The question usually ensures this.

### Free wins without cycles
- Any even number times any number ending in $5$ ends in $0$.
- An odd number times a number ending in $5$ ends in $5$.
- Every factorial from $5!$ on ends in $0$. So $1! + 2! + \cdots + 50!$ ends in $3$, from $1 + 2 + 6 + 24 = 33$.

### Power towers
For $7^{21^{20}}$ you need the exponent $21^{20}$ by $4$. Since $21$ leaves $1$ with $4$, so does $21^{20}$, and the unit digit is that of $7^1 = 7$. For $3^{4^5}$, the exponent $4^5$ is a multiple of $4$, so use $3^4$, giving $1$.

> **Tip:** For a tower, reduce the inner exponent first, then apply the outer cycle.

### Last two digits
For a base ending in $1$, like $71$ or $41$: the last digit stays $1$. The tens digit is the last digit of (tens digit of base times the exponent). For $71^{36}$: $7 \times 36 = 252$, keep $2$.
So the ending is $21$. For $41^{27}$: $4 \times 27 = 108$, keep $8$, ending $81$.

> **Example:** $6^{25} + 9^{31}$ ends in $6 + 9 = 15$, so the unit digit is $5$.

subtopics.notes:
A factor of a number divides it exactly. The factors of $12$ are $1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12$. A multiple is the reverse idea: $12, 24, 36, \ldots$ Every question here starts from the prime factorisation, so that skill comes first.

### Prime factorisation
Keep dividing by the smallest prime that fits. $720 = 2 \times 360 = 2 \times 2 \times 180 = \cdots = 2^4 \times 3^2 \times 5$. Write the result in power form $N = p^a \times q^b \times r^c$; every method below reads the exponents.

### Counting factors
A factor of $2^4 \times 3^2 \times 5$ chooses one power of each prime. The power of $2$: $0, 1, 2, 3$ or $4$, so five choices. The power of $3$: $0, 1$ or $2$, so three choices.
The power of $5$: $0$ or $1$, so two choices.

> **Rule:** Number of factors $= (a+1)(b+1)(c+1)$. For $720$: $5 \times 3 \times 2 = 30$ factors.

### Odd, even and special factors
- Odd factors: drop the power of $2$ completely. For $3600 = 2^4 \times 3^2 \times 5^2$: odd factors $= 3 \times 3 = 9$.
- Even factors: total minus odd, here $45 - 9 = 36$.
- Factors that are multiples of $k$: divide $N$ by $k$ and count factors of the result. For $1440$ with $k = 12$: $1440 \div 12 = 120 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5$, giving $16$.
- Perfect-square factors: every exponent may take even values only. Cube factors: $0, 3, 6, \ldots$

### Sum of factors
Write one bracket per prime and multiply.
$$\text{sum} = (1 + p + \cdots + p^a)(1 + q + \cdots + q^b) \cdots$$
For $360 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5$: $(1 + 2 + 4 + 8)(1 + 3 + 9)(1 + 5) = 15 \times 13 \times 6 = 1170$. For the sum of even factors only, start the bracket of $2$ at $2$: $(2 + 4 + 8) \times \cdots$

> **Tip:** The bracket form also answers sum of odd factors: just delete the bracket of $2$.

### Product of factors and factor pairs
Factors pair as $(1, N), (2, N/2), \ldots$ and each pair multiplies to $N$. So the product of all factors of $N$ is $N^{d/2}$ where $d$ is the factor count: for $12$, with $6$ factors, the product is $12^3 = 1728$.

The same pairing counts the ways to write $N$ as a product of two factors: $d/2$ ways when $N$ is not a perfect square, $(d+1)/2$ when it is. For two co-prime factors the answer is $2^{k-1}$, with $k$ the number of distinct primes.

### Trailing zeros of factorials
A trailing zero needs a $10 = 2 \times 5$. Factorials hold more twos than fives, so count the fives: divide by $5$, then the quotient by $5$ again, and add.

> **Rule:** Zeros in $n! = \left\lfloor \dfrac{n}{5} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \dfrac{n}{25} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \dfrac{n}{125} \right\rfloor + \cdots$. For $125!$: $25 + 5 + 1 = 31$ zeros.

### Highest power of a prime in a factorial
Same successive division by the prime. The power of $3$ in $100!$ is $33 + 11 + 3 + 1 = 48$. For a composite such as $12 = 2^2 \times 3$, find each prime's power, divide the power of $2$ by $2$, and take the smaller result. In $50!$: twos give $47$, so $23$ twos-pairs, and threes give $22$; the answer is $22$.

subtopics.title: Fractions, decimals & recurring decimals
subtopics.concept: A fraction compares a part with the whole; a decimal writes the same idea in place value. Every terminating or repeating decimal is a fraction in disguise, and converting between the two forms follows two fixed rules.

steps: Non-repeating digit: $2$ (one digit). Repeating block: $45$ (two digits).

subtopics.notes:
A fraction like $\dfrac{3}{4}$ means three parts out of four equal parts. The top number is the numerator, the bottom is the denominator. Fractions, decimals and percentages are three languages for the same quantity: $\dfrac{3}{4} = 0.75 = 75\%$.

### Comparing fractions in one step
Two rules save long division. Cross-multiplication: $\dfrac{a}{b}$ versus $\dfrac{c}{d}$, compare $ad$ with $bc$; the bigger product sits on the bigger fraction. Complement rule: if fractions sit close to $1$, compare what is missing. $\dfrac{13}{17}$ misses $\dfrac{4}{17}$, and $\dfrac{9}{11}$ misses $\dfrac{2}{11}$; since $\dfrac{4}{17} > \dfrac{2}{11}$, the first fraction is smaller. Equal numerators: the smaller denominator wins, because the same cake is cut into fewer pieces.

> **Tip:** Same numerator, smaller denominator: bigger fraction. Same denominator: bigger numerator wins.

### Converting a fraction to a decimal
Divide, and watch the remainders. If a remainder repeats, the digits repeat too. When the denominator (in lowest terms) has only $2$s and $5$s, the division must end.

> **Rule:** A fraction terminates only when its lowest-terms denominator equals $2^m \times 5^n$. Otherwise it repeats forever.

$\dfrac{9}{50} = \dfrac{18}{100} = 0.18$ terminates. $\dfrac{8}{13}$ must repeat, because $13$ has a prime factor other than $2$ or $5$.

### Repeating decimal to fraction
Pure repeating: numerator is the repeating block, denominator is as many nines as the block length. $0.\overline{7} = \dfrac{7}{9}$ and $0.\overline{72} = \dfrac{72}{99} = \dfrac{8}{11}$. Mixed, with non-repeating digits first: subtract. $0.4\overline{7} = \dfrac{47 - 4}{90} = \dfrac{43}{90}$ and $2.4\overline{7} = 2 + \dfrac{43}{90} = \dfrac{223}{90}$.

> **Rule:** All digits minus non-repeating digits, over as many nines as repeating digits followed by as many zeros as non-repeating digits.

### Adding repeating decimals
Convert each to a fraction first, then add. $0.\overline{7} + 0.\overline{3} + 0.\overline{2} = \dfrac{7 + 3 + 2}{9} = \dfrac{12}{9} = \dfrac{4}{3}$. With a common denominator of nine, the numerators simply add.

> **Watch:** Never add repeating decimals digit by digit; the shift between them breaks place value.

### Fraction of a quantity
"Two-fifths of a number" means multiply: $\dfrac{2}{5} \times N$. When a fraction of a number is given, divide to recover the number. If $\dfrac{2}{5}$ of a number is $48$, the number is $48 \times \dfrac{5}{2} = 120$.

> **Example:** $\dfrac{3}{5}$ of a number exceeds $\dfrac{1}{4}$ of it by $63$. Then $\left(\dfrac{3}{5} - \dfrac{1}{4}\right)N = \dfrac{7}{20}N = 63$, so $N = 180$.

### Continued fractions
A stack like $3 + \dfrac{1}{2 + \dfrac{1}{4}}$ unwinds from the bottom up: the innermost $\dfrac{1}{4}$ first, then the middle level, then add $3$. Keep every level as a fraction; never convert to decimals half way.

pyqPatterns.approach: Split a composite divisor into co-prime parts (72 = 8 × 9, 88 = 8 × 11). Apply the rule with fewest choices first — the last-three-digits rule of 8 or the alternating-sum rule of 11 — then the digit-sum rule. List the few cases; the asked quantity is usually the same in all of them.

example.q: If 8x6y4 is divisible by 88, find x + y.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Remainder when the new divisor is a factor of the old one
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'A number divided by 527 leaves 64. What is the remainder when it is divided by 17?'
pyqPatterns.approach: Check that the new divisor divides the old one. If it does, just divide the old remainder by the new divisor. This is a 20-second question.

example.q: N ÷ 195 leaves 47. Find N ÷ 15.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Remainder of large powers and products
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Huge powers such as $5^{70}$, $67^{67} + 67$ or products like $1021 \times 1023 \times 1025$ divided by a small number.
pyqPatterns.approach: Replace every number by its remainder (negative remainders are allowed). For powers, find a small power that leaves 1 or −1 and split the exponent. If the final result is negative, add the divisor.

example.q: Remainder of $67^{67} + 67$ divided by 68?

pyqPatterns.pattern: Unit digit of powers, products and sums
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Find the unit digit of $7^{95} \times 3^{58}$' or of a sum/difference of powers or a factorial sum.
pyqPatterns.approach: Keep only the unit digit of each base and the exponent mod 4 (remainder 0 means the 4th power). Multiply or add the unit digits. For a negative difference add 10. Factorials from 5! end in 0.

example.q: Unit digit of $2137^{754}$?

pyqPatterns.pattern: Number of factors, odd/even factors, sum of factors
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'How many factors does 720 have?', 'how many even factors …', 'sum of all factors of 360'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Prime-factorise. Number of factors = product of (power + 1). Odd factors: drop the 2. Sum of factors = product of brackets (1 + p + … + p^a).

example.q: How many odd factors does 3600 have?

pyqPatterns.pattern: Trailing zeros and highest power in n!
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'How many zeros are at the end of 125!?', 'largest n such that $3^n$ divides 100!'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Successively divide n by 5 (for zeros) or by the prime p and add all quotients. For a composite like 12 find the exponent of each prime part and take the smallest after dividing by the needed power.

example.q: Zeros at the end of 125!?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Expressions like $17^{25} + 23^{25}$ or $7^{24} - 1$ with 'is divisible by'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Odd power sum → divisible by (a + b). Difference → always divisible by (a − b), and by (a + b) too when the power is even. Match these with the options.

example.q: $19^{32} - 11^{32}$ is divisible by?

pyqPatterns.pattern: Recurring decimals to fractions and their sums
pyqPatterns.approach: Pure recurring: repeating digits over 9s. Mixed: (all digits − non-repeating digits) over (9s then 0s). Convert every term to a fraction before adding.

example.q: $0.4\overline{7} + 0.3\overline{5} = ?$

pyqPatterns.pattern: Counting multiples in a range and series sums
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'How many numbers between 200 and 600 are divisible by 4, 5 and 6?', 'sum of all three-digit multiples of 7'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Use floor division: multiples of k from a to b = ⌊b/k⌋ − ⌊(a−1)/k⌋. 'And' means LCM; 'or' means inclusion–exclusion. For sums use n/2 × (first + last).

example.q: How many integers from 1 to 1000 are divisible by neither 4 nor 6?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'If the digits are reversed the number increases by 27', 'a number is 4 times the sum of its digits'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Write the number as 10a + b. Difference with the reverse is 9(a − b); sum with the reverse is 11(a + b). Or test the options quickly.

example.q: A two-digit number is 4 times its digit sum; adding 27 reverses it. Find it.

solvedExamples.q: What is the unit digit of $3^{65} \times 6^{59} \times 7^{71}$?
solvedExamples.solution:
- $3^{65}$: $65 \bmod 4 = 1$ ⇒ unit digit of $3^1 = 3$.
- $6^{59}$: 6 raised to any power ends in 6.
- $7^{71}$: $71 \bmod 4 = 3$ ⇒ unit digit of $7^3 = 343$ is 3.
Product of unit digits: $3 \times 6 \times 3 = 54$ ⇒ unit digit **4**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Cyclicity 4 for 3 and 7: exponents 65 → 1, 71 → 3. Unit digits 3, 6, 3 → 3 × 6 = 18 → 8 × 3 = 24 → **4**.

solvedExamples.q: What is the remainder when $25^{25}$ is divided by 9?
Which of the following fractions is the largest? $\frac{5}{7}, \frac{7}{10}, \frac{9}{13}, \frac{11}{16}$
solvedExamples.shortcut:
All fractions are a bit above 2/3, so compare the gap from 1:
$1 - \frac{5}{7} = \frac{2}{7} \approx 0.286$, $\frac{3}{10} = 0.3$, $\frac{4}{13} \approx 0.308$, $\frac{5}{16} \approx 0.313$.
Smallest gap ⇒ largest fraction: $\frac{5}{7}$.

solvedExamples.q: The expression $3^{25} + 3^{26} + 3^{27} + 3^{28}$ is divisible by which of the following?
solvedExamples.solution:
Take out the common factor $3^{25}$:
$3^{25}(1 + 3 + 9 + 27) = 3^{25} \times 40 = 3^{25} \times 2^3 \times 5$.
30 = 2 × 3 × 5 — all present ✓. 16 needs $2^4$ (only $2^3$) ✗, 25 needs $5^2$ ✗, 11 absent ✗.
Answer: **30**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Factor the smallest power: bracket = 1 + 3 + 9 + 27 = 40. The number is 3^25 × 40, so any divisor must be built from 3s, at most three 2s and one 5 → 30.

solvedExamples.q: What is the sum of all two-digit numbers that are divisible by 6?
solvedExamples.solution:
Two-digit multiples of 6: 12, 18, …, 96.
Number of terms $= \frac{96 - 12}{6} + 1 = 15$.
Sum $= \frac{15}{2}(12 + 96) = 15 \times 54 = 810$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 15 terms (99 ÷ 6 = 16 minus the single-digit one, 6). Middle term = (12 + 96)/2 = 54. Sum = 15 × 54 = **810**.

practice.q: If the seven-digit number 74x5236 is divisible by 11, what is the value of x?
practice.solution:
Digits from the right: 6, 3, 2, 5, x, 4, 7.
Sum at odd places = 6 + 2 + x + 7 = 15 + x; sum at even places = 3 + 5 + 4 = 12.
Difference = (15 + x) − 12 = x + 3 must be 0 or 11 ⇒ x = 8.
practice.shortcut: x + 3 = 11 is the only possibility for a digit, so x = 8. Check option: 7485236 → (6+2+8+7) − (3+5+4) = 23 − 12 = 11 ✓.

practice.q: What is the unit digit of $7^{95} \times 3^{58}$?
A number when divided by 893 leaves a remainder of 193. What will be the remainder when the same number is divided by 47?
practice.solution:
Let $N = 893k + 193$. Since $893 = 47 \times 19$, $893k$ is a multiple of 47.
So the remainder is $193 \bmod 47$: $193 = 4 \times 47 + 5$ ⇒ **5**.
practice.shortcut: 47 divides 893, so just divide the old remainder: 193 − 188 = 5.

practice.q: The value of $2.4\overline{7}$ in the form $\frac{p}{q}$ is:
How many factors does 540 have?
practice.solution:
$540 = 2^2 \times 3^3 \times 5^1$.
Number of factors $= (2+1)(3+1)(1+1) = 3 \times 4 \times 2 = 24$.
practice.shortcut: Add 1 to each exponent and multiply: 3 × 4 × 2 = 24.

practice.q: What is the remainder when $2^{99}$ is divided by 17?
practice.shortcut: Find the ±1 power: $2^4 \equiv -1$. $2^{99} = (2^4)^{24} \times 2^3 \equiv (+1) \times 8 = 8$.

practice.q: How many zeros are there at the end of 250! (factorial 250)?
practice.solution:
Each trailing zero needs a pair (2, 5); 5s are fewer, so count the 5s.
$\left\lfloor \frac{250}{5} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \frac{250}{25} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \frac{250}{125} \right\rfloor = 50 + 10 + 2 = 62$.

practice.q: If the six-digit number 25x6y4 is divisible by 72, what is the value of x + y?
practice.solution:
72 = 8 × 9 (co-prime).
**By 8:** last three digits 6y4 must be divisible by 8. Checking y = 0 to 9: only 624 and 664 work ⇒ y = 2 or 6.
**By 9:** 2 + 5 + x + 6 + y + 4 = 17 + x + y must be a multiple of 9 ⇒ x + y = 1 or 10.
y = 2 ⇒ x = 8; y = 6 ⇒ x = 4. In both cases x + y = **10** (x + y = 1 is impossible since y ≥ 2).
practice.shortcut: Digit sum 17 + (x + y) → next multiple of 9 is 27 ⇒ x + y = 10 (x + y = 1 fails because y is 2 or 6).

practice.q: How many even factors does 1080 have?
practice.solution:
$1080 = 2^3 \times 3^3 \times 5$. Total factors $= 4 \times 4 \times 2 = 32$.
Odd factors (power of 2 = 0): $4 \times 2 = 8$.
Even factors $= 32 - 8 = 24$.
practice.shortcut: Force at least one 2: exponent of 2 has 3 choices (1, 2, 3) ⇒ $3 \times 4 \times 2 = 24$.

practice.q: How many numbers between 200 and 600 are divisible by 4, 5 and 6?
practice.solution:
Divisible by 4, 5 and 6 ⇔ divisible by LCM(4, 5, 6) = 60.
Multiples of 60 strictly between 200 and 600: 240, 300, 360, 420, 480, 540 ⇒ **6**.
practice.shortcut: $\left\lfloor \frac{599}{60} \right\rfloor - \left\lfloor \frac{200}{60} \right\rfloor = 9 - 3 = 6$. (600 itself is excluded — 'between'.)

practice.q: The number $47^{43} + 43^{43}$ is divisible by:
practice.solution:
For odd $n$, $a^n + b^n$ is divisible by $a + b$. Here $n = 43$ is odd ⇒ divisible by $47 + 43 = 90$.
Check traps: mod 4, $47 \equiv 43 \equiv 3$ ⇒ sum $\equiv 2 \times 3^{43} \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ — not divisible by 4. Mod 43 the sum $\equiv 4^{43} \equiv 4$ (Fermat), so 86 fails; similarly 94 fails.
practice.shortcut: Odd equal exponents + '+' sign ⇒ look for a + b = 90 in the options.

practice.q: What is the remainder when $1523 \times 1527 \times 1531$ is divided by 15?
practice.solution:
Reduce each number mod 15: 1523 → 8, 1527 → 12, 1531 → 1 (since 1515 = 15 × 101).
$8 \times 12 \times 1 = 96$, and $96 \bmod 15 = 6$.

practice.q: How many factors of $N = 2^4 \times 3^3 \times 5^2 \times 7$ are perfect squares?
practice.solution:
A factor is a perfect square only if every prime appears with an even exponent.
- 2: exponents 0, 2, 4 → 3 choices
- 3: exponents 0, 2 → 2 choices
- 5: exponents 0, 2 → 2 choices
- 7: exponent 0 only → 1 choice
Total $= 3 \times 2 \times 2 \times 1 = 12$.
practice.shortcut: Square factors = product of $\left(\left\lfloor \frac{a}{2} \right\rfloor + 1\right)$: $(2+1)(1+1)(1+1)(0+1) = 12$.

practice.q: What is the value of $0.\overline{3} + 0.\overline{47} + 0.1\overline{5}$?
How many numbers from 1 to 300 are divisible by 3 or 5 but NOT by 7?
practice.solution:
**Divisible by 3 or 5:** 100 + 60 − 20 (multiples of 15) = 140.
**Of these, divisible by 7 as well** (i.e. by 21 or 35): 14 + 8 − 2 (multiples of 105) = 20.
Required count = 140 − 20 = **120**.
practice.shortcut: Inclusion–exclusion twice: (3 or 5) − (21 or 35) = 140 − 20 = 120. Trap option 140 ignores the 'not by 7' condition.

practice.q: How many numbers between 1 and 500 are divisible by 7?
practice.solution: Multiples of 7 below 500: $\lfloor 499/7 \rfloor = 71$ (the largest is $7 \times 71 = 497$).

practice.q: How many integers from 1 to 1000 are divisible by neither 4 nor 6?
practice.solution:
Divisible by 4: 250. Divisible by 6: 166. Divisible by both = divisible by LCM 12: 83.
Divisible by 4 or 6 $= 250 + 166 - 83 = 333$.
Neither $= 1000 - 333 = 667$.
practice.shortcut: Use LCM 12 (not 4 × 6 = 24) for 'both'. Subtracting 250 + 166 directly gives the trap answer 584.

practice.q: How many three-digit numbers are divisible by 6 but not by 9?
practice.solution:
Three-digit multiples of 6: $\lfloor 999/6 \rfloor - \lfloor 99/6 \rfloor = 166 - 16 = 150$.
Those also divisible by 9 are multiples of LCM(6, 9) = 18: $\lfloor 999/18 \rfloor - \lfloor 99/18 \rfloor = 55 - 5 = 50$.
Required $= 150 - 50 = 100$.
practice.shortcut: 'By 6 but not 9' = multiples of 6 − multiples of 18.

practice.q: What is the value of $1^2 + 2^2 + 3^2 + \dots + 15^2$?
What is the value of $11^3 + 12^3 + 13^3 + \dots + 20^3$?
practice.solution:
Sum of cubes up to 20 $= \left[\frac{20 \times 21}{2}\right]^2 = 210^2 = 44100$.
Sum of cubes up to 10 $= 55^2 = 3025$.
Required $= 44100 - 3025 = 41075$.
practice.shortcut: Subtract the sum up to 10, not up to 11 (that gives the trap 39744).

practice.q: What is the sum of all three-digit numbers that are divisible by 7?
practice.solution:
First three-digit multiple = 105, last = 994.
Number of terms $= \frac{994 - 105}{7} + 1 = 128$.
Sum $= \frac{128}{2}(105 + 994) = 64 \times 1099 = 70336$.
practice.shortcut: Sum = number of terms × average of first and last = 128 × 549.5.

practice.q: What is the difference between the place values of the two 7s in 3,47,62,781?
practice.solution: The first 7 is in the lakhs place → 7,00,000. The second 7 is in the hundreds place → 700. Difference $= 7,00,000 - 700 = 6,99,300$.

practice.q: What is the product of the place values of the two 3s in 53,432?
practice.solution: In 53,432 the first 3 is in the thousands place (3000) and the second is in the tens place (30). Product $= 3000 \times 30 = 90,000$.

practice.q: How many prime numbers are there between 50 and 100?
practice.shortcut: Remember: 25 primes up to 100 and 15 up to 50, so 25 − 15 = 10.

practice.q: What is the sum of all prime numbers between 60 and 80?
practice.shortcut: Numbers ending in 1, 3, 7, 9 are the only candidates; strike out 63 (÷3), 69 (÷3), 77 (÷7).

practice.q: Which of the following is a rational number?
practice.solution: $\sqrt{8} \times \sqrt{2} = \sqrt{16} = 4$, which is rational. $\sqrt{3} + \sqrt{2}$, $2\pi$ and $\sqrt{5} - 1$ are all irrational.
practice.shortcut: Simplify each option first; only the one that becomes a perfect square root is rational.

practice.q: How many digits are needed to number the pages of a book having 350 pages?
practice.solution:
Pages 1–9: 9 digits. Pages 10–99: $90 \times 2 = 180$ digits.
Pages 100–350: $251 \times 3 = 753$ digits.
Total $= 9 + 180 + 753 = 942$.

practice.q: How many times does the digit 3 appear when all numbers from 1 to 100 are written?
practice.solution: Units place: 3, 13, 23, …, 93 → 10 times. Tens place: 30 to 39 → 10 times. (33 is counted in both, correctly, because it has two 3s.) Total 20.

practice.q: A total of 1,392 digits were used to number the pages of a book. How many pages does the book have?
practice.solution:
Digits used by pages 1–99 $= 9 + 180 = 189$.
Remaining digits $= 1392 - 189 = 1203$, each 3-digit page uses 3 → $1203 \div 3 = 401$ pages.
Total pages $= 99 + 401 = 500$.

practice.q: A two-digit number is 4 times the sum of its digits. If 27 is added to the number, its digits are reversed. Find the number.
practice.solution:
Let the number be $10a + b$.
$10a + b = 4(a + b) \Rightarrow 6a = 3b \Rightarrow b = 2a$.
Reversal adds 27: $9(b - a) = 27 \Rightarrow b - a = 3$.
So $a = 3, b = 6$ → number $= 36$.
practice.shortcut: Check options: 36 = 4 × 9 ✓ and 36 + 27 = 63 ✓.

practice.q: The sum of three consecutive even numbers is 162. What is the largest of them?
practice.solution: Middle number $= 162 \div 3 = 54$. Numbers: 52, 54, 56. Largest $= 56$.

practice.q: The sum of the digits of a two-digit number is 10. The number exceeds the number obtained by reversing its digits by 36. Find the number.
practice.solution:
Let the number be $10a + b$ with $a + b = 10$.
$(10a + b) - (10b + a) = 9(a - b) = 36 \Rightarrow a - b = 4$.
$a = 7, b = 3$ → number $= 73$.
practice.shortcut: Only 73 and 37 have digit sum 10 with gap 4; the number is bigger than its reverse, so 73.

practice.q: If the six-digit number 6x52y4 is divisible by 72, what is the value of x + y?
practice.solution:
$72 = 8 \times 9$.
**Rule of 8:** $2y4$ must be divisible by 8 → 224 or 264 → $y = 2$ or $y = 6$.
**Rule of 9:** digit sum $6 + x + 5 + 2 + y + 4 = 17 + x + y$ must be a multiple of 9 → $x + y = 1$ or $10$.
- $y = 2$: $x + y$ cannot be 1, so $x + y = 10$ → $x = 8$ (685224 ✓).
- $y = 6$: $x + y = 10$ → $x = 4$ (645264 ✓).
In both cases $x + y = 10$.
practice.shortcut: Digit sum 17 + (x + y) must reach 27 because y ≥ 2 rules out x + y = 1. So x + y = 10.

practice.q: If the five-digit number 8x6y4 is divisible by 88, what is the value of x + y?
practice.solution:
$88 = 8 \times 11$.
**Rule of 8:** $6y4$ divisible by 8 → 624 or 664 → $y = 2$ or $6$.
**Rule of 11:** from the right, odd places $4 + 6 + 8 = 18$ and even places $y + x$. So $18 - (x + y)$ must be 0 or 11 → $x + y = 18$ or $7$.
$x + y = 18$ needs $x = y = 9$, but $y$ is 2 or 6. So $x + y = 7$ (numbers 85624 and 81664 both work).
practice.shortcut: Rule of 11 gives x + y = 7 or 18; 18 is impossible here → 7.

practice.q: If the five-digit number 4x7y8 is divisible by 72, what is the value of $|x - y|$?
practice.solution:
**Rule of 8:** $7y8$ divisible by 8 → 728 or 768 → $y = 2$ or $6$.
**Rule of 9:** $4 + x + 7 + y + 8 = 19 + x + y$ must be 27 → $x + y = 8$.
$y = 2 \Rightarrow x = 6$; $y = 6 \Rightarrow x = 2$. In both cases $|x - y| = 4$.

practice.q: If the six-digit number 9x8475 is divisible by 11, what is the value of x?
practice.solution:
From the right: odd places 5, 4, x → $9 + x$; even places 7, 8, 9 → 24.
Difference $24 - (9 + x) = 15 - x$ must be 0 or 11 → $x = 4$.

practice.q: Which of the following numbers is divisible by 11?
practice.solution:
Use (odd-place sum) − (even-place sum), places counted from the right.
- 474881: odd places 1, 8, 7 → 16; even places 8, 4, 4 → 16; difference 0 ✓.
- 474871: 1 + 8 + 7 = 16 vs 7 + 4 + 4 = 15 → 1 ✗.
- 538921: 1 + 9 + 3 = 13 vs 2 + 8 + 5 = 15 → 2 ✗.
- 583261: 1 + 2 + 8 = 11 vs 6 + 3 + 5 = 14 → 3 ✗.

practice.q: The number $17^{25} + 23^{25}$ is divisible by:
practice.solution: $a^n + b^n$ with odd $n$ is divisible by $a + b$. Here $n = 25$ is odd, so it is divisible by $17 + 23 = 40$.
practice.shortcut: Odd power + sum → divide by (a + b). 6 = 23 − 17 would need a difference.

practice.q: Which of the following divides $7^{24} - 1$?
practice.solution:
$7^{24} - 1 = (7^2)^{12} - 1^{12}$, which is divisible by $7^2 - 1 = 48$.
It is not divisible by 49 or 56 (both are multiples of 7, but $7^{24} - 1$ leaves remainder $-1$ with 7), and not by 46.
practice.shortcut: $a^n - 1$ is divisible by $a^k - 1$ whenever $k$ divides $n$: $k = 2$ gives 48.

practice.q: $19^{32} - 11^{32}$ is divisible by:
practice.solution:
$a^n - b^n$ is always divisible by $a - b = 8$.
Since $n = 32$ is even, it is also divisible by $a + b = 30$.
So it is divisible by **both 30 and 8**.
practice.shortcut: Even power difference → both (a − b) and (a + b).

practice.solution: $5^{21}(1 + 5 + 25) = 5^{21} \times 31$. So the number is divisible by **31**.

practice.q: Which of the following is a factor of $2^{30} + 2^{31} + 2^{32} + 2^{33}$?
practice.solution: $2^{30}(1 + 2 + 4 + 8) = 2^{30} \times 15$. So **15** is a factor. The other options (13, 7, 9) do not divide $2^{30} \times 15$.

practice.q: What least number must be added to 8,357 so that the sum is exactly divisible by 12?
practice.solution: $8357 = 12 \times 696 + 5$. The remainder is 5, so add $12 - 5 = 7$. Check: $8364 = 12 \times 697$.
practice.shortcut: Trap: 5 is the number to subtract, not add.

practice.q: What is the largest five-digit number exactly divisible by 47?
practice.solution: $99999 = 47 \times 2127 + 30$. Subtract the remainder: $99999 - 30 = 99969$.

practice.q: What is the smallest six-digit number exactly divisible by 111?
practice.shortcut: Smallest n-digit multiple = 10…0 + (d − r).

practice.q: A six-digit number is formed by writing a three-digit number twice (for example 257257). Such a number is always divisible by:
practice.solution: $abcabc = abc \times 1000 + abc = abc \times 1001$ and $1001 = 7 \times 11 \times 13$. So it is always divisible by 7, 11 and 13.

practice.q: A three-digit number has all its digits equal (like 444). It is always divisible by:
practice.solution: $aaa = 100a + 10a + a = 111a = 3 \times 37 \times a$. So it is always divisible by **37**. (It is divisible by 27 only for some digits, e.g. 999.)

practice.q: A number when divided by 527 leaves a remainder of 64. What will be the remainder when the same number is divided by 17?
practice.solution: $527 = 17 \times 31$, so 17 is a factor of 527. Remainder $= 64 \bmod 17 = 64 - 51 = 13$.
practice.shortcut: Old remainder ÷ new divisor.

practice.q: A number divided by 84 leaves remainder 71. What is the remainder when the number is divided by 12?
practice.solution: 12 divides 84, so the remainder is $71 \bmod 12 = 71 - 60 = 11$.

practice.q: When a number is divided by 195 the remainder is 47. When the same number is divided by 15, the remainder is:
practice.shortcut: Trap: 47 itself is bigger than 15, so it cannot be the remainder.

practice.q: What is the remainder when $1021 \times 1023 \times 1025$ is divided by 17?
practice.solution: $1020 = 17 \times 60$, so the remainders are 1, 3 and 5. Product $= 1 \times 3 \times 5 = 15$, which is less than 17. Remainder **15**.
practice.shortcut: Spot 1020 = 17 × 60 and write each number as 1020 + small.

practice.q: What is the remainder when $1! + 2! + 3! + \dots + 100!$ is divided by 12?
practice.solution: From $4! = 24$ onwards every term is a multiple of 12. So only $1! + 2! + 3! = 1 + 2 + 6 = 9$ matters. Remainder **9**.

practice.q: What is the remainder when $3^{101}$ is divided by 8?
What is the remainder when $5^{70}$ is divided by 13?
practice.shortcut: Find a power giving −1; odd count of (−1) → divisor − 1.

practice.q: What is the remainder when $67^{67} + 67$ is divided by 68?
practice.shortcut: Base one less than divisor, odd power → −1.

practice.q: In a division sum, the divisor is 12 times the quotient and 5 times the remainder. If the remainder is 48, what is the dividend?
practice.solution:
Divisor $= 5 \times 48 = 240$. Quotient $= 240 \div 12 = 20$.
Dividend $= 240 \times 20 + 48 = 4848$.
practice.shortcut: Trap 4,800: forgetting to add the remainder.

practice.q: A number when divided by 68 gives quotient 269 and remainder 0. What will be the remainder when the same number is divided by 67?
practice.shortcut: $68 \times 269 = (67 + 1) \times 269$ → remainder $= 269 \bmod 67 = 1$.

practice.q: When a positive integer $N$ is divided by 7 the remainder is 3. What is the remainder when $N^3 + 2N$ is divided by 7?
practice.shortcut: Take N = 3 itself and divide directly.

practice.q: Two numbers, when divided by 17, leave remainders 13 and 11 respectively. What is the remainder when their product is divided by 17?
practice.solution: Product of remainders $= 13 \times 11 = 143 = 17 \times 8 + 7$. Remainder **7**.
practice.shortcut: Negative remainders: $(-4)(-6) = 24 \to 7$.

practice.q: A number when divided successively by 4 and 5 leaves remainders 1 and 4 respectively. What is the remainder when the number is divided by 20?
practice.solution:
Let the number be $N = 4q + 1$ and $q = 5k + 4$.
$N = 4(5k + 4) + 1 = 20k + 17$.
So $N$ leaves remainder **17** when divided by 20.
practice.shortcut: Remainder with product $= d_1 r_2 + r_1 = 4 \times 4 + 1 = 17$.

practice.q: What is the smallest number which, when divided successively by 3, 5 and 7, leaves remainders 2, 3 and 4 respectively?
practice.solution:
Work backwards. Last quotient = 0, so the number before division by 7 is 4.
Before division by 5: $5 \times 4 + 3 = 23$.
Before division by 3: $3 \times 23 + 2 = 71$.
Check: $71 = 3 \times 23 + 2$, $23 = 5 \times 4 + 3$, $4 = 7 \times 0 + 4$ ✓.

practice.q: What is the unit digit of $(2137)^{754}$?
practice.solution: Unit digit of base = 7. $754 \bmod 4 = 2$ → $7^2 = 49$ → unit digit **9**.
practice.shortcut: Only the last two digits of the exponent matter: 54 ÷ 4 leaves 2.

practice.q: What is the unit digit of $4^{63} \times 9^{72} \times 8^{41}$?
practice.solution:
- $4^{63}$: odd power → 4.
- $9^{72}$: even power → 1.
- $8^{41}$: $41 \bmod 4 = 1$ → 8.
Product $4 \times 1 \times 8 = 32$ → unit digit **2**.

practice.q: What is the unit digit of $(3694)^{1793} \times (615)^{317} \times (841)^{491}$?
practice.solution: $(3694)^{1793}$ ends in 4 (odd power of 4). $(615)^{317}$ ends in 5. $(841)^{491}$ ends in 1. $4 \times 5 \times 1 = 20$ → unit digit **0**.
practice.shortcut: Even × 5 → 0. No need to find exponents mod 4.

practice.q: What is the unit digit of $7^{105} - 3^{58}$?
practice.solution:
$105 \bmod 4 = 1$ → $7^{105}$ ends in 7.
$58 \bmod 4 = 2$ → $3^{58}$ ends in 9.
$7 - 9$ is negative, so borrow: $17 - 9 = 8$. Unit digit **8**.
practice.shortcut: Trap 2 comes from doing 9 − 7. The first number is bigger, so borrow 10.

practice.q: What is the unit digit of $2^{51} + 3^{52} + 4^{53} + 5^{54}$?
What is the unit digit of $1! + 2! + 3! + \dots + 50!$?
practice.solution: Every factorial from $5!$ onwards ends in 0. $1 + 2 + 6 + 24 = 33$ → unit digit **3**.

practice.q: What is the unit digit of $173 \times 346 \times 519 \times 721$?
practice.solution: Unit digits: $3 \times 6 = 18 \to 8$; $8 \times 9 = 72 \to 2$; $2 \times 1 = 2$. Answer **2**.

practice.q: What is the unit digit of the product $1 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 \times \dots \times 99$ (all odd numbers from 1 to 99)?
practice.solution: The product contains 5 and has no even factor. Odd × (number ending in 5) always ends in 5. So the unit digit is **5**, not 0 (0 needs a factor 2).

practice.q: What is the unit digit of $17^{17^{17}}$?
practice.solution:
We need the exponent $17^{17}$ divided by 4. $17 = 4 \times 4 + 1$, so every power of 17 leaves remainder 1 with 4.
So $17^{17^{17}}$ ends like $7^1$ → **7**.

practice.q: What is the unit digit of $8^{7^{6}}$?
practice.solution:
Exponent $7^6$: $7 \equiv -1 \pmod 4$ and 6 is even, so $7^6$ leaves remainder 1 with 4.
So $8^{7^6}$ ends like $8^1$ → **8**.

practice.q: What are the last two digits of $31^{786}$?
practice.shortcut: Base ends in 1: tens digit $= 3 \times 6 = 18 \to 8$; answer 81.

practice.q: What are the last two digits of $7^{2008}$?
How many factors does 720 have?
How many odd factors does 3600 have?
practice.solution: $3600 = 2^4 \times 3^2 \times 5^2$. Odd factors ignore the 2: $(2+1)(2+1) = 9$.
practice.shortcut: Trap 45 = all factors; 36 = even factors.

practice.q: How many factors of $2^6 \times 3^4 \times 5^3$ are perfect cubes?
practice.solution:
A perfect cube needs every power to be a multiple of 3.
- Power of 2: 0, 3, 6 → 3 choices.
- Power of 3: 0, 3 → 2 choices.
- Power of 5: 0, 3 → 2 choices.
Total $= 3 \times 2 \times 2 = 12$.

practice.q: How many factors of 1440 are divisible by 12?
practice.solution: $1440 \div 12 = 120 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5$. Factors of 120 $= 4 \times 2 \times 2 = 16$. Each gives one factor of 1440 divisible by 12.

practice.q: What is the sum of all the factors of 360?
What is the sum of all the even factors of 72?
practice.solution:
$72 = 2^3 \times 3^2$. An even factor must contain at least one 2.
Sum $= (2 + 4 + 8)(1 + 3 + 9) = 14 \times 13 = 182$.
practice.shortcut: All factors sum to 15 × 13 = 195; odd factors sum to 13; even = 195 − 13 = 182.

practice.q: How many zeros are there at the end of 125!?
How many zeros are there at the end of the product $5 \times 10 \times 15 \times 20 \times \dots \times 100$?
practice.solution:
The product $= 5^{20} \times (1 \times 2 \times \dots \times 20) = 5^{20} \times 20!$.
Number of 5s $= 20 + (20/5 + 20/25) = 20 + 4 = 24$.
Number of 2s (all come from 20!) $= 10 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 18$.
Zeros $=$ smaller count $= 18$.
practice.shortcut: Here 2s, not 5s, are the scarce factor.

practice.q: What is the largest value of $n$ such that $3^n$ divides $100!$?
What is the highest power of 12 that divides $50!$?
practice.solution:
$12 = 2^2 \times 3$.
Power of 2 in 50!: $25 + 12 + 6 + 3 + 1 = 47$ → number of $2^2$ blocks $= \lfloor 47/2 \rfloor = 23$.
Power of 3 in 50!: $16 + 5 + 1 = 22$.
Highest power of 12 $= \min(23, 22) = 22$.

practice.q: What is the product of all the factors of 36?
In how many ways can 360 be written as a product of two co-prime factors?
practice.solution:
$360 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5$ has 3 different primes. Each prime power must go completely to one factor.
Ordered splits $= 2^3 = 8$; unordered pairs $= 8/2 = 4$: $(1, 360), (8, 45), (9, 40), (5, 72)$.

practice.q: In how many ways can 360 be written as a product of two natural numbers (order not counted)?
practice.solution: $360 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5$ has $4 \times 3 \times 2 = 24$ factors. 360 is not a perfect square, so the factors pair up into $24 \div 2 = 12$ products.

practice.q: The value of $0.\overline{72}$ as a fraction in lowest terms is:
practice.solution: $0.\overline{72} = \frac{72}{99} = \frac{8}{11}$ (divide top and bottom by 9).
practice.shortcut: $\frac{18}{25} = 0.72$ exactly — that is the non-recurring trap.

practice.q: Express $3.1\overline{45}$ as a fraction.
practice.solution:
Whole part 3. Decimal part $0.1\overline{45}$: numerator $= 145 - 1 = 144$, denominator $= 990$ (two 9s for '45', one 0 for '1').
$\frac{144}{990} = \frac{8}{55}$. So $3.1\overline{45} = 3 + \frac{8}{55} = \frac{173}{55}$.

practice.q: What is the value of $0.\overline{6} + 0.\overline{7} + 0.\overline{8}$?
practice.shortcut: Adding digits (6 + 7 + 8 = 21 → 2.1) ignores the carries from the endless tail.

practice.q: What is the value of $0.4\overline{7} + 0.3\overline{5}$?
Which of the following fractions can be written as a terminating decimal?
practice.solution: $80 = 2^4 \times 5$ has only 2s and 5s, so $\frac{7}{80} = 0.0875$ terminates. The others have 7 ($14$), 3 ($45$, $24$) in the denominator.

practice.q: Which of the following fractions gives a NON-terminating (recurring) decimal?
practice.solution:
Reduce first:
- $\frac{21}{168} = \frac{1}{8}$ → terminates.
- $\frac{33}{60} = \frac{11}{20}$ → terminates.
- $\frac{17}{125}$, $125 = 5^3$ → terminates.
- $\frac{11}{48}$, $48 = 2^4 \times 3$ → **recurring** (factor 3).
practice.shortcut: Reduce before judging: 168 contains 3 and 7, but 21/168 = 1/8.

practice.q: Which of the following fractions is the largest?
practice.shortcut: Complements: $\frac{2}{5}, \frac{3}{8}, \frac{4}{11}, \frac{5}{14}$ = 0.40, 0.375, 0.364, 0.357. Smallest gap → largest fraction → $\frac{9}{14}$.

practice.q: Arrange in ascending order: $\frac{2}{3}, \frac{5}{7}, \frac{7}{10}, \frac{11}{15}$.
Which of the following fractions is the smallest?
practice.solution: Gaps from 1: $\frac{4}{17} \approx 0.235$, $\frac{3}{14} \approx 0.214$, $\frac{4}{19} \approx 0.211$, $\frac{2}{11} \approx 0.182$. The biggest gap belongs to $\frac{13}{17}$, so it is the smallest.
practice.shortcut: Complement method: biggest shortfall from 1 = smallest fraction.

practice.q: $\frac{3}{5}$ of a number is 63 more than $\frac{1}{4}$ of the number. What is the number?
practice.solution: $\left(\frac{3}{5} - \frac{1}{4}\right)x = 63 \Rightarrow \frac{7}{20}x = 63 \Rightarrow x = 180$.
practice.shortcut: Check: $\frac{3}{5} \times 180 = 108$, $\frac{1}{4} \times 180 = 45$, difference 63 ✓.

practice.q: Ravi spends $\frac{1}{3}$ of his salary on rent and $\frac{1}{4}$ of the remaining on food. He saves the rest, which is ₹9,000. What is his salary?
practice.solution:
After rent, $\frac{2}{3}$ is left. Food $= \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{2}{3} = \frac{1}{6}$ of the salary.
Savings $= 1 - \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$ of the salary $= ₹9,000$.
Salary $= ₹18,000$.
practice.shortcut: Trap ₹21,600: taking $\frac{1}{4}$ of the whole salary gives savings $\frac{5}{12}$.
